data.title: Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP) — viva
data.summary: Reactive & drug eruptions · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis (AGEP)** (Reactive & drug eruptions)_

**Q1. Define AGEP.**
- Acute severe cutaneous adverse reaction with rapid eruption of numerous small (<5 mm) non-follicular sterile pustules on oedematous erythema, fever and neutrophilia; >90% drug-induced

**Q2. Common culprit drugs.**
- Aminopenicillins (amoxicillin, ampicillin) and other β-lactams, macrolides, quinolones, pristinamycin, sulphonamides, hydroxychloroquine (long latency), terbinafine, diltiazem, calcium-channel blockers, ketoconazole, carbamazepine
- Non-drug triggers: infections (enterovirus, parvovirus B19, CMV, Mycoplasma), spider bites, mercury

**Q3. Clinical features.**
- Onset within 1–2 days of the drug (antibiotics; up to 1–3 weeks for some like HCQ)
- Burning/itchy erythema starting on face or intertriginous areas (axillae, groin) → spreads; hundreds of pinhead pustules; may have purpura, targetoid lesions, facial oedema; mucosal involvement mild in ~20% (only one site)
- Fever >38 °C, neutrophilia (>7×10⁹/L), mild eosinophilia; organ involvement (liver, kidney, lung) in ~20%
- Resolves in 1–2 weeks with collarette/punctate desquamation after stopping drug

**Q4. Pathogenesis.**
- Drug-specific T cells (CD4, CD8) release CXCL8 (IL-8), IL-17, IL-22, GM-CSF → neutrophil recruitment to epidermis — type IVd hypersensitivity
- IL36RN mutations in some patients (link with generalised pustular psoriasis)

**Q5. Histopathology.**
- Spongiform subcorneal and/or intra-epidermal pustules, papillary dermal oedema, perivascular infiltrate with neutrophils and eosinophils, necrotic keratinocytes; may have leukocytoclastic vasculitis
- Psoriasis features (regular acanthosis, tortuous vessels) absent

**Q6. Differentiate AGEP from generalised pustular psoriasis (GPP).**
- AGEP: drug history, acute onset (days), no personal/family history of psoriasis, rapid resolution in <15 days after stopping drug, eosinophils and necrotic keratinocytes on histology, positive patch test sometimes
- GPP: history of psoriasis, slower evolution, recurrent, longer duration, arthritis, psoriasiform histology, IL36RN mutations

**Q7. Other differentials of pustular eruption (PYQ: causes of pustular eruption).**
- GPP, subcorneal pustular dermatosis (Sneddon–Wilkinson — annular, flexural, chronic), IgA pemphigus, pustular vasculitis, DRESS with pustules, SJS/TEN early (pustular), bacterial folliculitis, candidiasis, pustular drug eruptions (acneiform, halogenoderma), infantile acropustulosis, erythema toxicum neonatorum, transient neonatal pustular melanosis

**Q8. Diagnostic score.**
- EuroSCAR AGEP validation score (morphology, course, histology): ≥8 definite, 5–7 probable, 1–4 possible, ≤0 no AGEP

**Q9. Management.**
- Stop the culprit drug (most important); supportive care — antipyretics, emollients, wet compresses
- Moderate/potent topical steroids for symptoms; systemic steroids (prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg) for severe disease or organ involvement; cyclosporine/infliximab rarely
- Avoid unnecessary antibiotics (pustules are sterile); patch test after recovery (positive in ~50%) — useful to confirm the drug
- Drug card and cross-reactivity counselling

**Q10. Prognosis.**
- Excellent; mortality ~1–5% mainly in elderly with comorbidities or organ involvement

**Q11. What is the patch test protocol for AGEP?**
- Patch test with suspected drugs (5–10% in petrolatum) 6 weeks–6 months after recovery on previously affected back; read at 48, 72, 96 h — pustular reaction at site confirms; positivity ~50%; delayed readings important

**Q12. Localised AGEP (ALEP).**
- Acute localised exanthematous pustulosis — pustules confined to face/ neck/ chest after drugs (amoxicillin, clindamycin) — same mechanism, milder

**Q13. Differentiate AGEP from DRESS with pustules.**
- DRESS: latency 2–8 weeks, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, atypical lymphocytes, internal organ involvement (liver), prolonged course >2 weeks; AGEP: latency <48 h (antibiotics), resolves in <2 weeks, neutrophilia

**Q14. Classify cutaneous adverse drug reactions by Gell–Coombs (revised).**
- Type I (IgE): urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis
- Type II (cytotoxic antibody): drug-induced pemphigus, immune thrombocytopenic purpura
- Type III (immune complex): serum sickness, vasculitis
- Type IV T-cell: IVa (Th1 — contact dermatitis), IVb (Th2/ eosinophils — DRESS, MPE), IVc (cytotoxic — SJS/TEN, FDE, MPE), IVd (neutrophilic — AGEP)
- Non-immune: pseudo-allergy (MRGPRX2), phototoxic, pigmentation, overdose/ side effects

**Q15. Why are antibiotics often wrongly continued in AGEP?**
- Fever with pustules and neutrophilia suggests sepsis, so antibiotics (often the culprit) are escalated — recognise sterile pustules (Gram stain/ culture negative), stop suspected drugs

## Quick spotter facts
- Hundreds of non-follicular pinhead pustules in flexures 1–2 days after amoxicillin — AGEP
- Resolves in <15 days with collarette desquamation

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Cutaneous adverse drug reactions); EuroSCAR AGEP validation score. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
